Period schedule:

Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Old Stag: Read-Aloud and First Impressions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp.43–46): teacher-led read-aloud of the prose story with new words.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the story title and the word 'stag.' Ask students what they know about forests and the animals that live in them, drawing on their own experience.
Let us Read (pp.43–46): read the prose story aloud with expression, pausing to explain new words — lush, hillock, tender, sheltering, recovery — as they appear in the text.
Shared reading: invite volunteers to read a paragraph each aloud while the class follows in their textbooks, and clarify any remaining unfamiliar words in context.
Whole-class discussion: ask students to name the main characters and describe the stag's hillock in their own words, anchoring understanding of the story's opening situation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage benefit from hearing the full story read fluently before they are asked to respond to it; model clear expression for the animal characters' emotions. The story's central conflict — illness worsened by the very friends who come to help — is worth pausing on briefly so students carry it into the comprehension work ahead.
materials: Blackboard or chart for new-word display

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: Why Did the Hillock Turn Bare?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.47): discuss and answer all four comprehension questions on the story.

time_bands.activity: Having read the prose story together, invite two students to retell the events in the story in their own words as a brief warm-up to the comprehension discussion.
Let us Think A (p.47): discuss questions 1 and 2 — why the stag was popular and why he could not go down the hillock — as a whole class, encouraging students to point to evidence in the text.
Let us Think A (p.47): discuss questions 3 and 4 — why the green cover vanished and how the animals realised and corrected their mistake — inviting paired discussion before sharing answers aloud.
Students write brief answers to all four questions in their notebooks; the teacher circulates and provides individual feedback on completeness and phrasing.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the story's read-aloud, students are ready to look closely at cause and effect — the grass disappearing because of greed is the heart of the moral. Watch for students who say the animals were bad without explaining the chain of events; guide them to trace what happened step by step.

periods.activity_title: Talking About Greed and Sharing: Discussion and the Jalebi Scenario

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.47): discuss whether the animals did the right thing and the effect of thinking only of one's own needs.
Let us Speak (p.53): discuss the jalebi scenario — fairness, sharing, and ensuring enough for everyone.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B (p.47): ask students whether the animals did the right thing in the end and why; take several responses and build a brief class discussion connecting their actions to the story's moral about sharing nature's resources.

Let us Think B (p.47): pose the second question — what would happen to green plants if everyone thought only of their own needs — and invite students to share their thoughts, linking it to the stag's hillock becoming bare.
Let us Speak (p.53): draw students' attention to the picture of children sharing a bowl of jalebis and introduce the four discussion questions about fairness and running out of something enjoyable.

Pairs share their responses to the jalebi questions with the class; the teacher draws parallels between the jalebi scenario and the animals' behaviour on the stag's hillock, consolidating the theme of wise resource use.

periods.teacher_notes: The jalebi scenario is an effective concrete anchor for the abstract idea of resource depletion; let students speak freely before guiding them to see the parallel with the story. Students who struggle to connect the two contexts can be helped by asking them what the bowl of jalebis and the hillock's grass have in common.

periods.activity_title: Descriptive Words and Adverbs: Building Precise Language

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.47): match story phrases to their meanings.
Let us Learn C (p.49): identify manner adverbs from a table and write sentences using them.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p.48): draw what comes to mind for 'lush forest', 'tender grass', and 'healthy food'.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn A (p.47): present the five phrase-meaning pairs from the story on the board and ask students to match them in their notebooks, then confirm answers with the class.

Let us Learn C (p.49): read the example sentence about the stag greeting his fellow animals 'warmly' aloud and explain that adverbs like 'warmly' describe how an action is done; students then work individually to encircle the manner adverbs from the table on the page.
Let us Learn C (p.49): in pairs, students write one sentence each for the adverbs they encircled, drawing on the story's events where possible; pairs share two or three sentences with the class.
Brief consolidation: ask students to name one descriptive phrase and one adverb they encountered today, connecting both to how authors make their writing more vivid and precise.

periods.teacher_notes: The distinction between adjectives (descriptive words in the phrase-matching task) and adverbs of manner is introduced together here because both deal with adding precision to language; keep the focus on how these words appear in the story rather than on isolated definitions. The homework drawing task for descriptive phrases can be shared briefly at the start of the next sitting to reinforce visual-verbal connection.

periods.activity_title: Writing in Voice: Speech Bubbles and a Paragraph About a Friend

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (pp.50–51): complete speech bubbles for the six-panel Monkeys' Fast picture-comic.
Let us Write B (p.52): complete the guided paragraph about a best friend using the sentence frame.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write A (pp.50–51): walk students through each panel of the Monkeys' Fast picture-comic, eliciting what is happening in each scene before they begin writing dialogue; model filling one speech bubble on the board together.

Let us Write A (pp.50–51): students write dialogue in the speech bubbles for all six panels independently; the teacher circulates and prompts students who are unsure by asking what the character in the picture might be thinking or saying.

Let us Write B (p.52): read the sentence frame aloud together and ask students to think of their best friend before they begin filling in the blanks; remind them to write in complete sentences where the frame allows.
Students complete the paragraph; two or three volunteers read their completed paragraphs aloud to the class, and the teacher acknowledges effective word choices or vivid details.

periods.teacher_notes: The speech-bubble task builds directly on the theme of self-control explored in the story — the monkeys face the same temptation as the animals on the hillock — so encourage students to draw on the story's moral when writing the concluding bubble. For the paragraph task, the sentence frame lowers the entry barrier; students who finish early can be asked to add one sentence of their own beyond the frame.

periods.activity_title: The Stag's Thank You Card: Drawing and Writing in Role

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.54): create a thank-you card from the stag — draw the front and write a message inside.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do (p.54): look at the illustration of the thank-you card together and invite students to recall how the animals helped the stag recover; briefly discuss what a heartfelt thank-you message should say and feel like.
Students draw the front of their card — the stag surrounded by forest friends — putting in at least three animals from the story and giving the scene a forest setting.

Students write the thank-you message inside their card, writing in the stag's voice; the teacher prompts them to mention the specific help received and express how it made the stag feel, using the prose story's ending as a guide.
A few students share their messages with the class; the teacher closes by connecting the stag's gratitude to the story's lesson about using nature's resources wisely and caring for one another.

periods.teacher_notes: Writing in role as the stag asks students to hold the whole story in mind — the illness, the grass disappearing, the friends' shame and eventual care — and express it through gratitude; this is a rich synthesis activity. Encourage students to use the descriptive phrases and adverbs they worked with earlier to make the message vivid.
materials: Blank card-sized paper or folded A4 sheets

items.item_stem: Why did the green grass on the old stag's hillock slowly disappear?

options.label: A
options.text: A long drought dried up all the plants on the hillock.

options.label: B
options.text: The visiting animals ate the tender grass while wishing the stag well.

options.label: C
options.text: The stag himself grazed on the grass as he tried to recover.

options.label: D
options.text: Other animals from a distant forest came and cleared the hillock.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have assumed weather caused the depletion without connecting the visitors' greed.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have misread the stag as an active agent rather than a helpless victim of others' greed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have invented an outside cause rather than tracing the cause within the story's events.

items.source_context: Old stag on hillock, animals' greed depleting grass, animals' remorse and recovery.
items.item_stem: The animals felt ashamed when they saw the hillock nearly bare. What did they decide to do, and what happened to the stag after that? Write two to three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The animals decided to stop eating the grass on the hillock, and some of them brought fresh leaves for the stag to eat. After good rains, the grass grew back, and the stag recovered his health.

items.source_lo: Student expresses reasoned opinions and connects a story's moral to real-life situations using a prose fable as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Animals' behaviour on the hillock, sharing resources, jalebi scenario paralleling resource depletion.
items.item_stem: Imagine a large bowl of fruit is placed in the middle of your classroom. Everyone takes a piece, but some children keep taking more and more. What do you think will happen to the fruit? Choose the statement that best describes what will happen.

options.text: If children keep taking more than their share, the fruit will run out before everyone has had enough.
Taking as much as you want is fine because there is always more fruit to replace it.
Sharing fairly means everyone gets some and the fruit lasts longer.
Only the fastest children deserve more fruit because they were quick enough to take it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1 and 3 are true. If children keep taking more than their share, the fruit will run out; sharing fairly ensures everyone gets some. Statements 2 and 4 are false because resources are limited and fairness, not speed, determines who gets a share.

items.item_stem: The animals in the story and the children sharing jalebis faced the same problem. Tell your teacher: what was that problem, and what is one thing you would do differently to make sure everyone gets enough?

expected_elements: Names greed or taking more than one's share.
Connects the story situation to the jalebi scenario.
Suggests a fair action, e.g. taking turns or limiting portions.

items.item_stem: Read the sentence below and choose the word that best completes it as a caption for the last panel of the Monkeys' Fast story: 'The monkeys _______ broke their fast and ate the bananas.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The blank should be filled with an adverb of manner, such as 'finally' or 'happily', showing the monkeys gave in to temptation at the end of the comic.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are the old stag. Create a thank-you card for the animals who helped you recover. Draw the front of the card and write a short message inside that says what the animals did for you and how it made you feel.

expected_elements: Front shows the stag with at least two forest animals.
Message names a specific act of care by the animals.
Message expresses the stag's feeling of gratitude.
